septic-tank-pumping.metaDescription: Septic tank pumping in Littlerock, California for rural homes, ranch parcels and orchard lots off Pearblossom Highway. Locally owned crew. Call us.
septic-tank-pumping.heroSub: We pump septic tanks on Littlerock ranch parcels and orchard lots, finding buried lids and working around horses, gates and dirt side roads off Pearblossom Highway.
paragraphs: Plenty of Littlerock homes date from a time when a smaller tank seemed like enough for the household living there. Families have grown, guest rooms have been added, and many of those original tanks now fill faster than the common three to five year guideline suggests. Older homes along Pearblossom Highway and out toward the foothills often have no written pumping history at all. A tank that goes too long sends solids into the seepage pit or leach field, and on these rural lots the disposal area is the hardest and most costly part of the system to replace.

Pumping here usually starts with finding the lid. Wind coming off the San Gabriel Mountains drops sand over everything, and on older lots the cover may sit well below the surface with no riser. Our crew digs it out, checks the liquid level before pumping, then empties the sludge and scum completely and looks at both baffles. On rocky ground near the foothills, reaching the lid takes more care, so we probe before we dig. Afterward we tell you how thick the layers were and suggest an interval that fits the number of people in the house and how water gets used.

Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and Littlerock is part of the east valley we cover. Before we head out, tell us which side road you are on, whether the gate locks, where the horses or dogs will be, and whether there is soft sand where a heavy truck could sink. Owners who run a fruit stand along the highway can pick a time that avoids their busiest hours. We give you a straight estimate on the phone or after a quick look at the site, then pump the tank and close everything up before we leave. Call us to set a time.

faqs.q: My Littlerock home is older and nobody knows the tank size. How often should I pump?
faqs.a: Without records, the first pumping is the best way to find out. Our crew measures the sludge and scum and notes the size of the tank, and from that we can suggest a sensible schedule. Many older Littlerock tanks are on the small side, so a household that has grown since the house was built may need service more often than the usual guideline. After that first visit you have a real number to plan around.

faqs.q: Can your truck reach a tank on an unpaved road off Pearblossom Highway?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Dirt side roads are a normal part of working in Littlerock, but loose sand and the low spots near washes can be soft, especially after storm runoff. When you call, describe the road surface, the gate width and how far the tank sits from where a truck can park. Long hose runs are common on big lots. If the road has washed out, we may suggest waiting until the ground firms up.

seepage-pit-pumping.metaDescription: Seepage pit pumping in Littlerock, CA for rural homes with slow or full pits in sandy and rocky foothill ground. Locally owned crew. Call to schedule.
seepage-pit-pumping.heroSub: In Littlerock, seepage pits sit in ground that shifts from loose desert sand to rock near the foothills, and we pump full pits and check how they recover.
paragraphs: Seepage pits do a lot of the work on Littlerock properties, because a deep pit can reach past the surface layer and fits on lots where horse pens, sheds and orchard rows already claim much of the yard. How a pit performs here depends on where it was dug. Down on the sandier flats, pits can drain well for a long time. Closer to the San Gabriel foothills, rock can limit how much soil surrounds the pit walls. When storm runoff sends the washes running, the ground around a pit can soak through, and the pit may fill faster than the tank feeds it.

Pumping a pit is not the same as pumping a tank. Our crew locates the pit cap, which is often buried and sometimes covered by years of wind-blown sand, and checks the liquid level against the inlet. We generally pump the septic tank on the same trip, since a full pit on an older Littlerock system often means solids have been slipping through. Once the pit is down, we watch the level closely. Water creeping back in from saturated ground, cracked rings near the top or a cap that has started to sag all shape what we tell you about its remaining life.

Older pits on Littlerock lots deserve some caution. Brick or block near the top can loosen, and a cap that sits in a horse path or under a parked trailer may have carried more weight than it should. We keep animals and kids clear of the opening, close it securely when we are done, and point out anything that looks unsafe. If the pit keeps refilling soon after pumping, we say so plainly and talk through options like an added pit. As a locally owned and operated company, Lancaster Septic Service gives you an honest estimate before the truck starts pumping.

faqs.q: Why does my Littlerock seepage pit fill up after a big storm?
faqs.a: Heavy rain is rare here, but when it comes off the mountains, washes run and the ground around a pit can soak through. Saturated soil cannot take effluent, so the pit holds it and the tank backs up behind it. Cut back on water use until the ground dries. If drains stay slow after things settle, have the tank and pit checked, since the storm may have exposed a pit that was already struggling.

faqs.q: My property near the foothills has rocky soil. Does that affect my seepage pit?
faqs.a: It can. Pits rely on the soil around and below them to absorb water, and rocky ground near the foothills may leave less soil for that job than sand on the flats. Some pits in those spots still work well for years, while others slow down sooner. Watching how the pit behaves after pumping gives us a better read, and adding a pit may be an option if one is not enough.

septic-inspection.metaDescription: Septic inspections in Littlerock, CA for home and ranch sales, older systems and buyers in escrow. Locally owned crew checks the tank and pit. Call us.
septic-inspection.heroSub: For Littlerock ranch and home sales, we open the tank, check the seepage pit or leach field and explain in plain terms how the system is holding up.
paragraphs: Rural property in Littlerock often changes hands with very little paperwork about the septic system. A house that has stood for decades may have a tank that was never upgraded, a seepage pit nobody has opened in years, or a leach field under what is now a horse pen. Buyers and lenders frequently ask for an inspection during escrow, and sellers benefit from knowing first. Los Angeles County Environmental Health may hold older records for some parcels, but many are thin, so the inspection itself becomes the most reliable account of what is actually in the ground.

An inspection here covers the whole route the wastewater takes. Our crew finds and opens the tank, measures sludge and scum, and checks the baffles and walls. We run water through the house to watch flow reach the tank. Then we turn to the disposal area, which on many Littlerock lots means a seepage pit with a buried cap, and look for standing water, odors or soft ground. Tanks on older lots here are sometimes smaller than a modern household needs, so we note the size and tell you whether it fits how the home will be used going forward.

Distance matters on an escrow schedule in Littlerock, so we plan the visit early and keep the agent in the loop when you ask. Give us the gate code, tell us about any livestock, and let us know whether someone can run the fixtures. Hold off on pumping beforehand, because an empty tank hides how the system has been behaving. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and our summary is written so buyers and sellers can both follow it. If repairs turn up, we explain them in plain terms and give an estimate so the deal can move forward on facts.

faqs.q: Is an inspection worth it on a Littlerock property with an older system?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Many Littlerock homes have systems that were installed decades ago and never upgraded, and records are often missing. An inspection tells you the tank size, the condition of the baffles and how the pit or field is draining. That helps a buyer plan for maintenance or repair, and it gives a seller answers before questions come up in escrow. Requirements for sales vary, so check with your agent and the county.

faqs.q: We added a second dwelling on our Littlerock lot. Should the inspection cover it?
faqs.a: Yes. A system sized for one older home can struggle when a second unit starts sending water to the same tank. Tell us about every building connected, and we will look at the tank size, the flow from each one and how the pit or field is coping with the combined load. Los Angeles County may have its own expectations for added units on a parcel, so it is worth checking with Environmental Health as well.

septic-repair.metaDescription: Septic system repair in Littlerock, CA for broken baffles, cracked lids and damaged lines on older rural systems. Locally owned crew. Call for an estimate.
septic-repair.heroSub: Older Littlerock systems wear out one part at a time, and we track down the broken baffle, cracked lid or crushed line before we dig anything up.
paragraphs: Septic lines on Littlerock ranch lots lead a hard life. Horse trailers, feed deliveries and tractors cross yards where the pipe between the house and tank may sit only a short way down, and loose sandy soil gives it little support. Over time a joint separates or a section cracks, and drains start to slow. Inside older tanks, concrete baffles corrode until they break off, letting scum drift toward the seepage pit. On a system that has passed through several owners, there may also be old patches nobody remembers, so the first job is working out what actually failed.

Finding the problem before digging saves a lot of yard. We listen to what you have noticed, open the tank and check the level and the baffles. If the line from the house is the suspect, a camera run shows where it broke or sagged. On rocky ground near the foothills, knowing the exact spot matters even more, because every hole takes real effort. Typical Littlerock repairs include a new outlet tee or baffle, a replacement lid, a cut-out and replaced pipe section, or a reset distribution box. You hear what we found and what the fix involves before any work starts.

Weather plays a part too. Summer heat and cold mountain nights work on exposed pipe and old concrete lids, and wind can push sand into covers that no longer seal. After a repair, we suggest small changes that help, such as keeping trailers off the line route or adding a riser so a cracked lid is not hidden again. As a locally owned and operated outfit, we put a clear estimate in front of Littlerock owners before any digging. Some repairs may bring Los Angeles County requirements into play, and we can explain what Environmental Health might ask for. Call us to set up a visit.

faqs.q: My horse trailer drives over the septic line. Could that be why my drains are slow?
faqs.a: It may be. Repeated weight over a shallow line in loose soil can crack a pipe or pull a joint apart, and waste then collects at the low spot. A camera inspection shows whether the line is damaged and exactly where. Once it is repaired, plan a route for trailers and equipment that stays clear of the tank and pipe, and consider marking the line so visitors know where not to drive.

faqs.q: Should I repair an old Littlerock system or replace it?
faqs.a: Often a single failed part is the real problem, and repair makes sense. A new baffle, lid or pipe section can keep an older system running well for a long time. If the tank is badly cracked, collapsing or far too small, or the seepage pit no longer takes water after pumping, replacement may be the better answer. We look at the whole system and tell you honestly which situation you are in before you spend money.

leach-field-repair.metaDescription: Leach field repair in Littlerock, CA for soggy ground, slow drains and fields worn down by livestock or rocky soil. Locally owned crew. Call us today.
leach-field-repair.heroSub: We repair Littlerock leach fields that have stopped absorbing, whether the trouble is sealed soil, a tilted distribution box or trenches trampled by livestock.
paragraphs: On larger Littlerock lots, a leach field may run under ground that has since become a horse turnout, a feed storage area or a path for farm equipment. Hooves and wheels compact the soil and can crush pipe that sits only a short way below the surface. Closer to the foothills, rock limits how far trenches can spread, so fields there were often built tight to begin with. Add solids from a tank that went years between pumpings, and the trench bottoms seal with biomat until effluent has nowhere to go except up toward the surface.

Repair begins at the tank, because a broken outlet baffle or an overdue pumping is often what ruined the field. Our crew checks for liquid flowing back from the trenches, opens the distribution box to check that flow splits evenly, and probes the field to find which runs are saturated. A camera can show crushed or root-clogged laterals. Depending on what turns up, the fix may be jetting the lines, resetting the box, resting part of the field, or adding trenches in ground that still drains. On the sandy flats there is often more room to work with than on rocky foothill lots.

Storms that send water down the washes can saturate a field that was already marginal, so we also look at how runoff moves across the property and whether grading could keep it off the trenches. Until the repair is done, fence animals away from wet ground and spread out laundry. Bigger field projects can bring county review into the picture, and Los Angeles County Environmental Health is the place to check for your parcel. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and we give you a plain estimate after looking at the field in person. Call us before the wet spots spread further.

faqs.q: Can I keep horses on the area over my leach field?
faqs.a: It is best not to. Hooves compact the soil over the trenches and can crack shallow pipe, and a compacted field absorbs less water. Manure and urine also add moisture to ground that is already handling effluent. If your Littlerock lot is tight on space, ask us to locate the field so you can fence it off and move pens or turnouts to another part of the property.

faqs.q: Is there enough room on a rocky foothill lot to add trenches?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Rock near the foothills limits where trenches can go, so we look at which parts of the lot still have workable soil and how much space sits clear of wells, buildings and property lines. In some cases a seepage pit fits better than more trenches. Los Angeles County may require soil testing or review before a new disposal area is built, so we walk through what may apply once we have seen the site.

septic-installation.metaDescription: Septic installation and replacement in Littlerock, CA for new rural homes and worn-out systems on sandy or rocky lots. Locally owned crew. Call us.
septic-installation.heroSub: Building on open Littlerock land or replacing a decades-old system, we help plan a tank and seepage pit or leach field that suits your soil and lot.
paragraphs: With public sewer limited in Littlerock, most new homes on vacant parcels need their own septic system, and many older homes are reaching the point where the original one cannot keep up. Tanks put in decades ago were sometimes sized for a smaller household than the one living there now, and replacement is a chance to correct that. The choice between a leach field and one or more seepage pits depends on what a soil evaluation shows, and here the ground can swing from loose sand on the flats to rock near the San Gabriel foothills.

Planning comes before digging. Our crew visits the lot to look at the house plans or the old system, setbacks from wells and property lines, and where a heavy machine can get in from the road. Littlerock parcels often carry barns, sheds and animal areas, and the disposal area needs to stay clear of all of them, plus any spot where you may build later. Los Angeles County may require a design, soil testing, review and inspections before a new system is put in service, so check with Environmental Health early, and we can walk through what it may ask for.

On install day we excavate, set the tank level on firm ground, connect the lines and build the pits or trenches to the approved layout. Rocky spots near the foothills can slow excavation, and we plan for that. Risers go on so lids sit at grade instead of disappearing under blown sand, and we backfill and grade so storm runoff moves away from the system. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated. You receive a clear estimate after the site visit, along with an explanation of how the old tank and pit will be handled if one is being replaced.

faqs.q: Does Littlerock have sewer I could connect to instead?
faqs.a: Public sewer is limited in Littlerock, and most homes rely on a private septic system. Whether a sewer line reaches a particular parcel is a question for Los Angeles County, so it is worth asking before you plan a new system or a major repair. For most rural lots here, a properly sized septic tank with a seepage pit or leach field is the practical option, and we can help you think through which one fits.

faqs.q: We want to add a shop and more horse pens later. How does that affect the septic layout?
faqs.a: It matters a lot. The tank, pipe and disposal area need to stay clear of buildings, driveways and animal areas, and a field under a future pen will get compacted. Sketch out where you expect the shop, pens and any added parking to go before the system is designed. On a big Littlerock lot there is usually room for everything if it is planned together, and we can talk through the layout during the site visit.

septic-risers.metaDescription: Septic riser and lid installation in Littlerock, CA. Bring buried tank lids to grade on windy rural lots and stop digging every visit. Call our crew.
septic-risers.heroSub: Wind off the San Gabriel Mountains buries Littlerock tank lids in sand, so we raise them to grade with sealed risers and lids that fasten down.
paragraphs: Wind sweeping down from the mountains carries sand across open Littlerock lots and drops it over anything low to the ground, including septic lids. On older systems those lids were never brought up to grade in the first place, so finding them means digging, and near the foothills that digging runs into rocky ground. A riser fixes this once. It extends the tank opening to the surface, and a sealed lid keeps sand and dust from working into the tank. That matters on a property where the tank may sit well out from the house along an unmarked route.

We usually add risers during a pumping, since the lids are already exposed. Our crew checks the tank top and opening, fits an adapter, and builds the riser in sections to the right height, sealing each joint. The lid fastens down with screws or a lock, which matters on property where horses, dogs, children and visitors move around freely. Some Littlerock owners like the lid a few inches above grade so it stays visible after a windstorm, while others want it flush where equipment passes nearby, as long as no vehicle drives directly over it.

Risers also help when a property changes hands, since an inspector can open the tank right away instead of hunting through sand and rock. If nobody knows where the tank sits, we locate it first. Being locally owned and operated, we keep the estimate simple, covering the risers, the lids and any pumping done at the same time. Tell us whether you want gravel, pavers or bare soil put back around the lid, and where gates and animals will be on the day of the work. Call us to plan the visit.

faqs.q: Will a riser lid stay put in Littlerock's wind?
faqs.a: A properly installed lid will. The ones we use are heavy and fasten down with screws or a lock, so wind cannot lift them and sand cannot blow in around a loose edge. Sand may still drift over a flush lid during a windy stretch, which is why some owners choose a lid set slightly above grade. A quick sweep after a strong blow keeps it easy to spot when the next pumping comes around.

faqs.q: Can you install a riser on an older tank in rocky ground near the foothills?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Rock makes the digging slower, but once the opening is exposed, the riser attaches to the tank top the same way it would anywhere else. We check the condition of the concrete around the opening first, since older tanks can have worn or crumbling edges. If the tank top is damaged, we explain what needs fixing before a riser goes on, so the new lid sits on a sound base.

grease-trap-pumping.metaDescription: Grease trap pumping in Littlerock, CA for kitchens along Pearblossom Highway, many of them on septic. Locally owned crew. Call us to plan regular service.
grease-trap-pumping.heroSub: For food businesses along Pearblossom Highway in Littlerock, we pump grease traps on a schedule that keeps grease out of the septic tank and seepage pit.
paragraphs: Food businesses in Littlerock sit mostly along Pearblossom Highway, and like the homes around them, many are not on public sewer. That changes the stakes of a neglected grease trap. Grease that slips past the trap does not disappear into a city main. It cools inside the tank, joins the floating scum and can drift out to the pit or field, sealing the soil it touches. A kitchen that keeps its trap pumped protects a system that would be costly and disruptive to replace on a commercial lot along the highway.

Kitchen volume rarely stays level through the year, so a pumping interval that worked in a slow month may fall short when business picks up. Our crew measures the grease and solids layers each visit, pumps the trap or interceptor out completely, and scrapes the caked grease off walls and baffles. The inlet and outlet tees and the lid get a look as well, and if the business is on septic we can look at the tank on the same trip. Each service ends with a dated record of what was removed, ready for your files or an inspector.

Small kitchens along the highway cannot shut down for a pump-out at lunch, so we schedule before opening or after closing. Tell us whether the trap sits under a sink or as an in-ground interceptor outside, and keep the lid area clear of parked cars. A health or sewer agency may set its own pumping rules, and those differ from business to business, so ask Los Angeles County Environmental Health what applies to you. We are a locally owned and operated crew, and we quote the trap and any septic work alongside it before starting. Call us to set a schedule.

faqs.q: My Littlerock kitchen drains to a septic tank. Should the trap be pumped more often?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Grease that slips through on a septic property lands in your own tank and may move on to the pit or field, so there is less room for error than on a sewer line. Many owners in that position choose a shorter interval. Our crew checks the layer depths every visit and recommends a schedule that fits your cooking and trap size, and the county may have its own expectations as well.

faqs.q: Do I need a grease trap for a small food stand on the highway?
faqs.a: It depends on what you cook and how the wastewater is handled. A stand that only sells produce may not need one, while a business that fries or cooks with oil usually does. Requirements vary, so check with Los Angeles County Environmental Health about your specific setup. If a trap is needed or already installed, we can pump it on a regular schedule and keep a service record for you.

emergency-septic-service.metaDescription: Emergency septic service in Littlerock, CA for backups, overflowing tanks and full seepage pits on rural lots. Call and we will send a truck out.
emergency-septic-service.heroSub: Sewage backing up in a Littlerock home or pooling over a seepage pit cannot wait, so call and we will send a truck as soon as we can.
paragraphs: Some of the worst septic problems in Littlerock follow heavy storms off the San Gabriel Mountains. Washes run, the ground around a seepage pit or leach field soaks through, and a system that was barely keeping up suddenly has nowhere to send water. Drains back up into the lowest tub or shower, or effluent rises near the tank. Other emergencies come from a full tank on an older home, a crushed line under a trailer path, or a failed pump. Each one gets worse with every flush, so the first step is to stop using water right away.

Distance is part of the planning on a Littlerock emergency call. When you call, tell us your side road, the gate setup, where animals are, and whether recent rain has softened the ground where a truck would park. That helps us bring the right hose length and reach you without getting stuck. On site, our crew pumps the tank or pit until the house drains are moving, then works back through the inlet line, baffles, any pump and the disposal area to find what set it off. You hear what happened before we pack up.

While you wait, keep people and animals away from any sewage in the yard, and do not let dogs or livestock drink standing water near the tank. Hold off on the washer, showers and flushing. A sounding pump alarm calls for a breaker check, but leave the chamber lid closed. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and we take Littlerock backups seriously because a rural household without a working bathroom has few easy options. You get an estimate before any repair beyond the emergency pump-out. Call us and we will get a truck headed your way as soon as we can.

faqs.q: Why did my Littlerock septic back up right after a big rain?
faqs.a: Heavy storms are rare here, but when water comes off the mountains, it can saturate the soil around a seepage pit or leach field. Wet ground cannot absorb effluent, so it backs up into the tank and then the house. Cut water use, steer runoff around the tank and pit if you can, and call us if drains stay slow. A storm backup often points to a pit or field that was already near its limit.

faqs.q: What should I do about livestock near a septic overflow?
faqs.a: Move horses and other animals away from the area and keep them from drinking any standing water nearby. Effluent carries bacteria that can make animals sick. Fence or block off the wet spot if you can, and keep children away too. Once our crew pumps the system down and finds the cause, we can suggest how to clean up the area and when it makes sense to let animals back.

septic-line-jetting.metaDescription: Septic line jetting and camera inspection in Littlerock, CA for slow drains, roots and crushed lines on rural lots. Locally owned crew. Call to book.
septic-line-jetting.heroSub: Long sewer lines on Littlerock lots clog, sag or crack under heavy loads, so we jet them clean and show you camera footage of the inside.
paragraphs: On a big Littlerock parcel, the line from the house to the tank may run a long way, and the outlet line to a seepage pit or leach field can be even longer. Every foot is a chance for trouble. Orchard and shade trees on older properties send roots toward any loose joint, sandy soil lets pipe settle into low spots where waste collects, and heavy loads from trailers or equipment can crack or crush a shallow section. A snake might poke through a clog for a while, but it rarely tells you why the line keeps slowing down.

Our crew usually starts with the camera. We enter through a cleanout or the tank and follow the line, watching for roots, cracks, sags and separated joints. If the pipe is sound, we choose a nozzle and pressure that suit it and jet the line, washing grease, sludge and roots back toward the tank, then run the camera again to confirm it is clear. When the footage shows damage, a locator on the camera head lets us mark the spot and depth on the ground, which saves a lot of digging on rocky foothill lots.

Line work fits naturally with other service on a Littlerock visit. Jetting pushes debris into the tank, so pumping at the same time makes sense, and the camera can also confirm where the line runs if the tank location is unknown. Tell us which drains are slow, whether trees or a trailer path sit near the line, and where any cleanouts are. Lancaster Septic Service is locally owned and operated, and you see the footage with us before deciding on any repair. We give a clear estimate for the jetting and any fix the camera points to. Call us to book a visit.

faqs.q: We have old fruit trees near the house. Can their roots get into the septic line?
faqs.a: They can. Trees on older Littlerock properties often have roots that have spread for years, and septic lines carry the water they are looking for. Roots usually enter at a joint or crack, then grow into a mass that catches waste. Jetting cuts them out of the pipe, and the camera shows where they got in, so you can decide whether to repair that section or keep the line on a cleaning schedule.

faqs.q: Can a camera find where my line goes on a large lot?
faqs.a: Yes. The camera head carries a small transmitter, and a receiver above ground follows it, so we can trace the path and depth of the line across the property. That is useful on big Littlerock lots where the tank or pit sits well away from the house, or where nobody knows which way the line runs before planning a barn, fence or driveway near the house.

septic-tank-locating.metaDescription: Septic tank locating in Littlerock, CA for rural homes and ranch lots where lids are buried under sand or rock. Locally owned crew marks lids. Call us.
septic-tank-locating.heroSub: On Littlerock lots where the tank could be anywhere between the house and the back fence, we trace the line, find the lids and mark them for you.
paragraphs: Plenty of Littlerock owners have never seen their septic tank. The house may be decades old, the system never upgraded, and the only clue a faded receipt from a previous owner. Since then, sheds, pens and gravel pads may have gone up around it, and wind off the mountains has laid sand over any marker that once existed. Knowing where the tank is matters before pumping, before an escrow inspection, and before building a barn, setting fence posts or bringing in heavy equipment, because a tank or line can crack under weight it was never meant to carry.

The search begins at the foundation, where the plumbing heads out toward the yard. We feed a small transmitter down the line from a cleanout, then walk the signal across the lot with a handheld receiver, which shows the path, the depth and the spot where the line meets the tank. We confirm with a steel probe, though rocky ground near the foothills can make probing slower and less precise. Then we dig to expose the lids. If the transmitter cannot get through, we can try a different entry point or trace back from a known seepage pit cap on the property.

Once the tank is found, each lid gets a flag or a paint mark, plus measurements taken off a house corner or a fence post, and we draw a simple map you can file with your property records. Many Littlerock owners pair locating with pumping or risers, so nobody has to go hunting for that tank again. Our company is locally owned and operated, and the estimate is settled before anyone digs. Let us know about gates, animals, sprinkler or water lines and recent projects in the yard. Call us to schedule tank locating at your place.

faqs.q: Does Los Angeles County have records of where my Littlerock tank is?
faqs.a: It might. Los Angeles County Environmental Health may hold permits or drawings for some parcels, especially for systems installed or replaced more recently. Older Littlerock systems often have thin or missing records, though, and even a drawing may not match what was actually built. It is worth asking the county, but tracing the line on site is usually the surest way to find the tank.

faqs.q: My tank might be under a horse pen. Can you still find it?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The transmitter signal passes through soil and gravel, so we can trace the line under a pen and pinpoint where the tank sits. Expect to move animals and possibly some panels so we can dig to the lids. Once it is found, think about relocating the pen, since hooves and weight over a tank are hard on the lids and the tank top over the long run.
